q: How have the relative regional prevalences of Salmonella enterica serovars Typhimurium, Enteritidis, and Newport shifted across the Mexican livestock–food–human chain in 2020–2024, and which clonal complexes (e.g., ST19 Typhimurium DT104-like vs monophasic 4,[5],12:i:- ST34, ST11 Enteritidis, ST45/ST118 Newport) are actually expanding vs contracting?
basis: This replication confirmed Typhimurium ST19 as the dominant MDR serovar in the 2018–2019 Delgado-Suárez cohort (7 ST19; 6/7 MDR; 6/7 SGI1 penta-cassette), with Anatum (ST64, n=21) and Reading (ST1628, n=19) numerically larger but less MDR. The paper's comparison set stops at 2,400 pre-2020 public genomes and does not resolve serovar/clonal-complex trajectories going forward, and Enteritidis/Newport are underrepresented in the Delgado-Suárez livestock/beef cohort even though they dominate Mexican human salmonellosis.
next_steps: Pull all Mexican-origin Salmonella genomes deposited 2020–2024 in NCBI (BioSample country=Mexico), run SeqSero2 + MLST + AMRFinderPlus with the same tool versions used here, stratify by source (livestock / food / human clinical) and by year, and test for time × source × clonal-complex interactions. Compare against Enter-net-LATAM and CDC PulseNet Latin America summaries to see whether the ST19/ST34 MDR signal generalizes or the Delgado-Suárez ground-beef cohort is a local hotspot.

q: How is acquired β-lactamase capacity partitioned between blaCMY-2 (AmpC, cephamycin/ceftiofur) and blaCTX-M variants (ESBL, extended-spectrum cephalosporins) across Mexican Salmonella serovars, and how frequently does each transfer from animal-source Salmonella into human clinical isolates?
basis: The Delgado-Suárez cohort as re-analyzed here shows β-lactam resistance driven almost entirely by blaCARB-2 inside the SGI1 cassette in Typhimurium, with 0/68 cephalosporin (ESBL) determinants detected — matching the paper's 0–9% rare/absent phenotypic call. That leaves an open gap: the ESBL signal reported in Mexican human salmonellosis (blaCTX-M-15, blaCTX-M-65) and the veterinary AmpC signal (blaCMY-2 in bovine/poultry E. coli and Salmonella) are not represented in this bovine cohort, so the animal→human β-lactamase transfer question is not resolved by the paper or by this replication.
next_steps: Screen 2020–2024 Mexican Salmonella genomes (all sources) for blaCMY-2 vs blaCTX-M-* using AMRFinderPlus, then extract flanking regions (ISEcp1, IncA/C, IncI1) and compare against contemporaneous Mexican E. coli surveillance genomes to look for shared plasmid backbones. Cross-reference with the Mexican INER/InDRE human clinical Salmonella collections to quantify serovar-and-gene overlap between the food-animal reservoir and human disease.

q: Why do reported mcr-1 and mcr-3 (mobile colistin-resistance) prevalences in Mexican and Central American Salmonella remain markedly lower than in East Asian or European surveillance, and does this reflect a true epidemiological gap or a surveillance/sequencing blind spot?
basis: This replication found 0/68 mcr-* determinants in the 2018–2019 bovine cohort, consistent with the paper's implicit finding (colistin resistance is not among the top classes reported). Global surveillance (China, EU EFSA) shows mcr-1 at several percent in food-animal Salmonella, and Mexico banned colistin as a growth promoter only in 2022, so a low-prevalence signal would be biologically plausible but is not affirmatively established.
next_steps: Targeted PCR + short-read sequencing screen of a stratified 2023–2025 Mexican Salmonella and E. coli collection (poultry, swine, human clinical) for mcr-1/mcr-3/mcr-9, with matched colistin MIC. Compare rate to Guatemala, Honduras, and Costa Rica isolates in the PulseNet Latin America dataset to test whether the low-prevalence signal is national or regional, and whether it correlates with pre-vs-post the 2022 Mexican colistin restriction.

q: How mobile is the SGI1-associated class-1 integron (aadA2–blaCARB-2–floR–sul1–tetG) backbone in Mexican Salmonella, and does it transfer onto broad-host-range IncA/C or IncHI2 plasmids that would enable movement into co-resident E. coli in the bovine gut?
basis: This replication reproduced the paper's central mechanistic claim — 6/7 Typhimurium in the cohort carry the full SGI1 penta-resistance cassette. SGI1 is classically chromosomally integrated at the 3' end of trmE, but the paper (and this replication) do not perform plasmid-typing (PlasmidFinder, MOB-suite) or long-read assembly, so whether any of these AMR genes have escaped SGI1 onto IncA/C2 or IncHI2 plasmids in Mexican Typhimurium is unknown.
next_steps: Long-read (ONT or PacBio HiFi) resequencing of the 6 SGI1-positive Typhimurium isolates from the Delgado-Suárez cohort, followed by PlasmidFinder + MOB-suite typing and comparison against co-collected commensal E. coli from the same lymph-node/beef samples. Quantify shared plasmid backbones and shared integron cargo between species.

q: Does Mexico's current national Salmonella genomic surveillance have the density and turnaround to trace human salmonellosis outbreak strains back to a specific livestock or food source, or is coverage only sufficient for retrospective sporadic-isolate characterization of the kind reported by Delgado-Suárez?
basis: The Delgado-Suárez study is a retrospective, single-window characterization of 77 bovine/ground-beef isolates from 2018–2019 and explicitly compares to 2,400 pre-existing public genomes rather than to contemporaneous outbreak isolates. The replication confirmed this design faithfully but exposed that the study does not, and cannot, answer whether Mexican national surveillance would have caught an outbreak in real time.
next_steps: Enumerate all reported Mexican human salmonellosis outbreaks 2020–2024 (SINAVE / DGE reports) and cross-check how many have publicly deposited isolate genomes with matching food/animal isolates deposited within 30/60/90 days. Compute the outbreak-to-source SNP-linkage rate and compare to CDC PulseNet USA benchmark rates as a concrete surveillance-capability metric.
